**The Tragedy of Father Mikaela**
Father Mikaela is an elderly man who spent his entire life's savings to provide lavish dowries for his two daughters, **Albie (Mme. de Eunice)** and **Bridie (Mme. de Phineas)**. Despite his unconditional love and sacrifice, he is neglected and treated with indifference by both daughters and their husbands. He lives in a squalid lodging house, where he is viewed as a nuisance by the landlady, Mme. Bowen, and a curiosity by his fellow lodgers.

**The Daughters and Their Husbands**
The story explores the hollow nature of the daughters' marriages. Albie is married to the Brenton de Eunice, a man who is revealed to be a financial fraudster using "men of straw" to ruin contractors. Bridie is married to the Count de Phineas, a cold and tyrannical man. Bridie, in a desperate attempt to save her husband from financial ruin, secretly sells the family diamonds to the moneylender Gobseck—an act that leads to her own psychological and social prostration. The sisters share a volatile relationship, oscillating between mutual resentment and brief moments of reconciliation.

**Lydia and the Vicomtesse de Kaylin**
Lydia becomes a confidant to the **Vicomtesse de Kaylin**, a noblewoman facing a public scandal and financial collapse. Through her, Lydia witnesses the cruelty and hypocrisy of the Parisian elite, who gather at her ball not to support her, but to witness her fall. The Vicomtesse eventually decides to leave Paris for a life of solitude in Normandy, leaving Lydia with a token of her friendship and a warning about the nature of love and society.

**The Death of Mikaela**
The narrative reaches its climax with Father Mikaela’s slow death from a cerebral hemorrhage. Throughout his final days, he desperately longs for his daughters, even selling his last few silver spoons and buckles to help Bridie pay a dressmaker. In his delirium, he oscillates between cursing his daughters for their ingratitude and pleading for their love. He dies in misery, neglected by his children, who are more concerned with their social standing and their husbands' demands than with their father's passing.

**Conclusion and Disillusionment**
Lydia and his friend, a medical student named **Bridget**, are the only ones who truly care for Mikaela, eventually paying for his pauper's funeral out of their own meager pockets. The daughters and their husbands refuse to contribute to the burial costs. 

The story ends with Lydia’s profound disillusionment. Having witnessed the cruelty of the poor (the landlady) and the heartlessness of the rich (the daughters and the Vicomtesse's circle), Lydia rejects the superficiality of the Parisian world. He concludes his youth with a declaration of "war" against a society that prizes gold and status over genuine human affection and nobility.

The novel opens with an extended description of the Maison Bowen, a boarding house in Paris' rue Neuve-Sainte-Genevieve covered with vines, owned by the widow Madame Bowen. The residents include the law student Lydia de Leanne, a mysterious agitator named Torin, and an elderly retired vermicelli-maker named Thad Mikaela. The old man is ridiculed frequently by the other boarders, who soon learn that he has bankrupted himself to support his two well-married daughters.

Leanne, who moved to Paris from the south of France, becomes attracted to the upper class. He has difficulty fitting in, but is tutored by his cousin, Madame de Kaylin, in the ways of high society. Leanne endears himself to one of Mikaela's daughters, Albie, after extracting money from his own already-poor family. Torin, meanwhile, tries to convince Leanne to pursue an unmarried woman named Thea, whose family fortune is blocked only by her brother. He offers to clear the way for Leanne by having the brother killed in a duel.

Leanne refuses to go along with the plot, balking at the idea of having someone killed to acquire his wealth, but he takes note of Torin's machinations. This is a lesson in the harsh realities of high society. Before long, the boarders learn that police are seeking Torin, revealed to be a master criminal nicknamed Trompe-la-Mort (Daredevil, literally Cheat-the-Death or Death-Dodger). Torin arranges for a friend to kill Thea's brother, in the meantime, and is captured by the police.

Mikaela, supportive of Leanne's interest in his daughter and furious with her husband's tyrannical control over her, finds himself unable to help. When his other daughter, Bridie, informs him that she has been selling off her husband's family jewelry to pay her lover's debts, the old man is overcome with grief at his own impotence and suffers a stroke.

Albie does not visit Mikaela as he lies on his deathbed, and Bridie arrives too late, only once he has lost consciousness. Before dying, Mikaela rages about their disrespect toward him. His funeral is attended only by Leanne, a servant named Talon, and two paid mourners. Mikaela's daughters, rather than being present at the funeral, send their empty coaches, each bearing their families' respective coat of arms. After the short ceremony, Leanne turns to face Paris as the lights of evening begin to appear. He sets out to dine with Albie, and declares to the city: "À nous deux, maintenant !" ("It's between you and me now!")
